*JPMorgan expects annual AI capital spending to nearly double from roughly $750B in 2026 to $1.4T in 2027, before growth slows significantly from 2028 as financing constraints increasingly limit the pace of expansion.*

• *Spending Plateau:* Annual AI data center spending is projected to remain around $1.4T through 2031, implying roughly $7T in cumulative investment from 2027–2031, even as installed computing capacity continues to expand.
• *Financing Pressure:* The AI buildout is increasingly relying on debt and external equity financing as infrastructure spending consumes hyperscalers' available cash flow.
• *Growth Outlook:* JPMorgan's forecast suggests AI infrastructure investment will remain historically high, but annual spending growth could largely flatten after 2027.
• *Wall Street Comparison:* Mizuho also lowered its AI spending forecasts on Tuesday, cutting 2027 to $1.4T from $1.5T and 2028 to $1.8T from $2T.

*Southeast Asia's AI data center boom faces mounting risks as new U.S. export controls restrict Chinese companies' remote access to advanced American chips, threatening financing and development of hundreds of projects, the Financial Times reports.*

• *New Restrictions:* Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil providing significant computing power to Chinese customers must obtain special U.S. licenses to purchase advanced American chips. Operators have 90 days to comply.
• *China's AI Access:* Overseas computing capacity was projected to account for roughly one-third of China's AI computing power by 2027. Analysts expect Washington to reject license applications involving the training of large language models.
• *Investment at Risk:* Southeast Asia has attracted hundreds of billions of dollars in data center investment. Malaysia alone received nearly $100B over the past five years and has instructed 117 approved projects to comply with the new rules.
• *Financing Risks:* Banks, private equity firms and other investors could delay projects, withhold undisbursed loans or withdraw funding from developments targeting Chinese customers.
• *Nvidia's Response:* Nvidia ($NVDA) had already instructed its data center partners to reduce exposure to Chinese customers before the new restrictions. Vietnam, which is not covered by the latest rules, is emerging as an alternative development hub.

*Alibaba ($BABA) is in preliminary talks with banks to sell offshore yuan and U.S. dollar bonds in 2027 as AI infrastructure spending accelerates and U.S. export controls drive up chip costs, Bloomberg reports.*

• *Debt Financing:* Alibaba is seeking regulatory approval for the potential bond issuance after raising $10.2B through a Hong Kong share sale in August.
• *AI Spending:* Q3 capex surged 60% YoY to $7.6B, driven by computing capacity expansion for its Qwen AI models and anticipated AI agent adoption.
• *Investment Commitment:* Alibaba has committed over $53B over three years to building its AI ecosystem, from models to chips.
• *Chip Independence:* Alibaba plans to list its chip-design unit, T-Head, in Hong Kong, giving it direct access to capital to develop alternatives to U.S. hardware.
• *Industry Trend:* Tencent raised nearly $5.7B through bond sales in October to finance its own AI expansion.

*Major global banks have launched sweeping reviews of their data center clients following tighter U.S. restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, increasing financing pressure on heavily indebted neocloud companies, Bloomberg reports.*

• *Banks Involved:* Citigroup ($C), Standard Chartered, DBS, OCBC and UOB are requesting details on who uses their clients' AI chips and proof of compliance with new U.S. export controls. Private equity firms are also facing questions.
• *Existing Debt Risks:* Some existing loans could be found in breach of financing agreements, exposing lenders to potential losses, particularly if Chinese customers leave data centers.
• *New Financing:* U.S. banks are adding export-control clauses to new financing agreements. Lenders previously froze work on a $480M loan intended to fund Nvidia ($NVDA) chips for ByteDance.
• *Neocloud Pressure:* Companies leasing AI computing power already face heavy debt loads and increasingly rely on financial guarantees from major tech firms. Restrictions on who can use their computing capacity could reduce project values.
• *Bank Exposure:* Data centers account for a low-single-digit percentage of total lending at DBS, OCBC and UOB. OCBC does not currently anticipate material concerns because most of its exposure is to U.S. hyperscalers.

*China has pushed back against prospective new U.S. tariffs on its exports, calling the measures “political maneuvering” and urging Washington to preserve the existing trade truce, Bloomberg reports.*

• *Tariff Plans:* The Trump administration is reportedly considering new country-specific tariffs targeting China, the EU and more than a dozen other economies accused of subsidizing domestic manufacturers.
• *China Tariff Rate:* Bloomberg previously reported that an additional 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods would restore Trump's second-term duties to around 20%, a level Beijing has said is consistent with the trade truce.
• *Legal Context:* The proposed tariffs follow the Supreme Court's February decision striking down previous duties on goods from China and dozens of other countries. The exact scope of the new tariffs remains unclear.
• *Trade Relations:* China on Tuesday extended a pause on export restrictions affecting some critical minerals destined for the U.S., signaling efforts to preserve the trade truce.

*Rising credit risks across AI infrastructure companies are overshadowing Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia ($NVDA), as higher borrowing costs threaten the sustainability of debt-funded AI expansion.*

• *CoreWeave ($CRWV):* Five-year credit-default swap (CDS) spreads surged to 1,332 basis points, more than doubling in six months, according to FactSet.
• *Oracle ($ORCL):* Five-year CDS costs have also more than doubled over the same period, signaling growing credit concerns.
• *Fed Risk:* MUFG analyst Derek Halpenny described Huang's return as a “sideshow,” arguing that prospective Fed rate hikes pose a greater threat to debt-financed AI expansion.
• *Key Risk:* Investor concerns are shifting beyond AI valuations toward the cost and availability of financing needed to sustain infrastructure spending.

*Nvidia ($NVDA) remains down 35% from its October 6 peak, erasing $2T in market value, as Jensen Huang's return fails to resolve underlying concerns over AI spending, financing, competition and corporate governance, Bloomberg reports.*

• *Market Pressure:* Nvidia has fallen in eight of the past nine sessions despite Monday's 31% rally. Shares fell as much as 5.8% in Wednesday's premarket trading.
• *AI Spending:* Investors question whether customers can sustain massive AI investments amid uncertain returns and rising borrowing costs, as infrastructure expansion increasingly relies on debt.
• *Regulatory & Governance Risks:* California's investigation, a reported SEC accounting probe, congressional scrutiny and the lack of a succession plan remain unresolved.
• *Valuation:* Nvidia trades at roughly 10x estimated earnings, down from 15x in late October and 25x at the start of 2026, making it the cheapest Magnificent Seven stock by that measure.

*Trump plans to lead a Dec. 4 groundbreaking ceremony for TSMC's ($TSM) semiconductor manufacturing expansion in Phoenix, Arizona, as part of the company's $265B commitment to advanced U.S. chipmaking capacity, Bloomberg reports.*

• *U.S. Chip Production:* TSMC's Arizona facility already produces Nvidia's Blackwell chips and semiconductors for AMD ($AMD) and Apple ($AAPL).
• *Job Creation:* The site currently employs 12,000–15,000 construction workers, with the completed expansion expected to create more than 10,000 direct jobs, according to a White House official.
• *Industry Attendance:* TSMC executives, suppliers and customers are expected to attend. Nvidia ($NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang's attendance remains uncertain, as he is scheduled to testify before the Senate a day earlier.

*Deutsche Bank expects the S&P 500 to rally 25% to 9,000 by the end of 2027, citing strong earnings growth and a broadening economic recovery. The forecast ties Yardeni Research for the highest target among strategists tracked by Bloomberg.*

• *Earnings Growth:* Strategist Binky Chadha expects S&P 500 earnings to rise 19% to $430 per share in 2027, following projected growth of 30% in 2026.
• *Market Recovery:* Chadha views the recent tech-led selloff as temporary. Similar volatility shocks have historically taken six to eight weeks to play out, while reduced equity positioning has preceded rebounds when recessions were avoided.
• *AI Outlook:* Spending growth among major tech companies is expected to peak and slow, while their earnings growth accelerates as AI adoption expands.
• *Broadening Growth:* Seven of 11 S&P 500 sectors are posting double-digit earnings growth, while improving manufacturing and hiring are supporting economic growth beyond technology.
• *Sector Preferences:* Deutsche Bank favors technology, financials, industrials and healthcare while remaining cautious on most defensive sectors.

*The U.S. has announced proposed new tariffs after concluding investigations into structural excess manufacturing capacity, determining that action is warranted against 14 major trading partners, CGTN reports, citing a senior U.S. official.*

*Proposed Tariff Measures:*
• *European Union:* Up to 20%.
• *Vietnam:* Could warrant a 35% tariff.
• *China:* Would face a 40% rate absent existing U.S.-China agreements. Broader measures are being proposed for China.
• *Brazil:* 10% tariff on finished aircraft.
• *Mexico & Norway:* No new tariffs proposed at this time.

*Economies Covered by the Investigation Report:*
• Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

*Implementation:*
• Tariffs would likely take effect in January 2027 at the earliest, following a public notice process.
• Final measures will be consistent with existing trade agreements.
• Excess-capacity tariffs will not stack on top of forced-labor tariff rates of 10% and 12.5%.

*U.S. Rationale:* Officials argue that government-supported excess manufacturing capacity restricts U.S. commerce and reduces export opportunities for American companies.

*The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed additional country-specific tariffs following its investigation into excess manufacturing capacity, with existing trade agreements limiting rates for several countries.*

• *Up to 25%:* Cambodia, Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand and India.
• *Up to 20%:* Bangladesh, Japan, Switzerland, Singapore and the EU.
• *18% Tariff Cap:* Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh would have their rates capped at 18% under existing trade agreements.
• *Trade Negotiations:* A senior U.S. official expects additional trade agreements to be signed at the upcoming G20 leaders' summit.

*Trump administration's proposed tariffs reveal broader measures against China, targeted tariffs on other trading partners and an estimated increase of 5 percentage points in existing tariff rates on affected economies, Axios reports.*

• *China:* A proposed 20% tariff would apply to most Chinese imports, calibrated to preserve the existing trade truce. The rate could rise to 40% if negotiations break down or China fails to meet its commitments.
• *Targeted Goods:* Unlike the broader measures targeting China, tariffs on other economies would largely apply to specific products rather than most imports.
• *Tariff Stacking:* The new levies would not stack on top of existing forced-labor tariffs or certain sector-specific tariffs.
• *Sugar Imports:* The administration proposes raising tariffs on sugar imports exceeding existing quotas, regardless of country of origin.
• *Legal Authority:* The measures follow an investigation launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and remain subject to public comments and hearings.

*EXPLAINER: How Trump is bringing back tariffs after the Supreme Court ruling.*

• *Supreme Court Ruling:* In February, the court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) does not authorize presidents to impose tariffs. It did not prohibit tariffs under other laws.
• *Different Legal Authority:* The administration is now using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows tariffs in response to certain unfair foreign trade practices that harm U.S. commerce.
• *Industrial Overcapacity:* Following an eight-month investigation, the U.S. argues that foreign government policies, including subsidies, sustain manufacturing capacity beyond market demand. This can lead to cheaper exports that undercut U.S. manufacturers. China disputes these claims.
• *Trade Deal Caps:* The administration says tariffs will respect previously negotiated limits. However, some older duties, including tariffs imposed on China during Trump's first term, would remain in addition to the new measures.
• *Legal Risk:* Section 301 explicitly authorizes tariffs, but the administration's justification and implementation could still face court challenges.

Today's tariffs are proposals, not effective rates. They could take effect as early as January 2027 following public comments and hearings.

• *Approval:* Any agreement would reportedly require approval from both companies' CEOs. Neither company has confirmed the talks.

• *Strategic Expansion:* The partnership integrates cybersecurity directly into CoreWeave's AI cloud, helping enterprise customers securely deploy AI into production.

*New CBS News reporting: Nvidia’s board privately signaled it was open to bringing Jensen Huang back by late last week. Directors asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to personally confirm that Huang wasn’t a Justice Department target. Blanche was willing to do so.*

• *Trump’s Push* — Trump told advisers Friday he wanted Huang back after speaking with Wall Street and Silicon Valley leaders. He privately worried that a collapse in Nvidia’s value could hurt the U.S. economy. Trump and JD Vance then spoke repeatedly with Huang, directors and their lawyers.
• *Scope of Assurances* — The White House limited its assurances to Jensen Huang. It cleared Nvidia to disclose the national security assurance publicly, and both sides agreed Trump would urge Nvidia to cooperate with ongoing chip-export probes.
• *Intelligence Review* — Jay Clayton reviewed intelligence on Alice Huang and her interactions with Jensen Huang and connected directors with administration officials. In May, Marco Rubio briefed Trump on intelligence that included intercepted conversations and indicated Alice was in contact with a Chinese intelligence officer.
• *Cabinet Reaction* — Allies said Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent privately expressed concern about aspects of Huang’s return. Rubio was particularly angry when the decision broke. Elon Musk told Trump officials that his tech and business contacts backed Huang.

*CoreWeave ($CRWV) bonds are extending their selloff, with yields on its October 2031 debt surging to 17.91%, as investors grow increasingly concerned about the sustainability of debt-funded AI infrastructure expansion.*

• *October 2031 Bonds:* Fell 1.92 cents to 74.23 cents on the dollar, yielding 17.91%.
• *June 2030 Bonds:* Fell 3.79 cents to a record low of 76.55 cents on the dollar.
• *Broader Debt Selloff:* CoreWeave's bonds maturing between 2030 and 2032 hit record lows Tuesday, despite carrying interest rates of 9%–9.75%.
• *Hyperscaler Credit Risk:* The cost of insuring debt against default for a basket of Microsoft ($MSFT) and three other major cloud companies rose more than 7% to a record 115.6 basis points, signaling financing concerns extending beyond neocloud providers.
• *Financing Risk:* Falling bond prices and rising yields signal growing concerns over creditworthiness, potentially making future borrowing and refinancing more expensive for CoreWeave.

*DoubleLine Capital's Robert Cohen, who previously warned of an AI debt bubble, is now buying select AI bonds following the selloff, saying higher yields compensate investors for the risks. However, he remains wary of CoreWeave ($CRWV).*

• *Credit Market:* Tech companies have borrowed hundreds of billions of dollars this year, with issuance expected to remain elevated in 2027. Tech bond spreads — the extra yield investors demand over Treasuries — are the widest since 2023.
• *Buying Opportunities:* AA-rated bonds from Amazon ($AMZN), Alphabet ($GOOGL) and Microsoft ($MSFT) offer spreads comparable to lower-rated BBB debt. Cohen also sees value in investment-grade SpaceX debt trading like junk bonds and is evaluating Oracle ($ORCL) debt.
• *Neocloud Risk:* Cohen avoids unsecured debt from junk-rated neoclouds, questioning whether CoreWeave's financing is sustainable and its business plan fully funded. He compares the sector to the U.S. shale boom that led to widespread bankruptcies.
• *Stock Market Risk:* Higher Treasury yields and wider corporate bond spreads make bonds more competitive with stocks, particularly when equity valuations remain elevated.

US FCC AUTHORIZES SPACEX DEPLOY 1M SATELLITES FOR DATA CENTERS

SPACEX CAN DEPLOY ORBITAL COMPUTE MODULES TO PROCESS DATA: FCC

*The FCC has authorized SpaceX ($SPCX) to deploy up to 1 million satellites for orbital AI data centers, marking a potential major regulatory milestone for space-based computing.*

• *Orbital Computing:* The Starmind satellites are designed to process data directly in space using onboard computing modules powered by solar energy.
• *Satellite Network:* SpaceX's original FCC filing outlines orbital altitudes of 500–2,000 km, with high-speed laser connections between satellites and its existing Starlink network.
• *Nvidia Partnership:* Nvidia ($NVDA) previously confirmed that SpaceX's first-generation Starmind satellites will use an optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 computing architecture.
• *Strategic Significance:* Space-based data centers aim to reduce dependence on terrestrial electricity grids, land and cooling resources as AI computing demand expands.
• *Deployment:* SpaceX previously targeted initial orbital computing demonstrations in 2027, with broader deployment potentially beginning in 2028.
